gas.label: gas/pre
gas.text: These notes collect a few short facts about ideal gases for testing the chunker.

gas.label: gas/v2/1-na
gas.text:
Avogadro proposed that equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. One mole of any ideal gas therefore occupies the same molar volume, and the number of molecules per mole is the Avogadro constant, about six times ten to the twenty three.

An ideal gas is a model in which the molecules are point particles that never interact except in brief elastic collisions. Its pressure, volume and temperature obey the ideal gas law, PV = NkT, where N is the number of molecules and k is the Boltzmann constant. The model works well for dilute gases far from condensation, such as helium or argon at room temperature and ordinary pressure, and it is the reference system against which real gases are compared in the rest of these notes here.

gas.label: gas/v2/1-bc
gas.text:
Boyle observed that at constant temperature the pressure of a fixed amount of gas is inversely proportional to its volume: halving the volume of the container doubles the pressure. Charles found that at constant pressure the volume grows linearly with temperature. Both empirical laws are special cases of the ideal gas law and were historically the evidence that led to it, long before the molecular picture of a gas was accepted by chemists.

Real gases deviate from this simple behaviour at high density, where molecules are close together.

gas.label: gas/v2/1-d
gas.text: The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal gas law for two effects that the ideal model ignores. First, molecules occupy a finite excluded volume, so the volume available to each molecule is reduced by a constant b per mole. Second, molecules attract one another at moderate distances, which lowers the pressure exerted on the walls by an amount proportional to a over the square of the molar volume. The resulting equation of state predicts a critical point, below whose temperature the isotherms develop a loop that signals the coexistence of liquid and vapour. Maxwell's equal area construction replaces the loop by a flat segment at the vapour pressure. The van der Waals constants a and b are fitted to measured critical data for each substance, and the theory then gives a qualitative account of condensation, although the predicted critical compressibility ratio is not accurate for most real fluids.

gas.label: gas/1-e
gas.text: Kinetic theory explains the ideal gas law from the motion of molecules. In equilibrium the molecular speeds follow the Maxwell distribution, whose shape depends only on the temperature and the molecular mass. The mean kinetic energy per molecule is three halves of kT, independent of the mass, so heavier molecules move more slowly on average. The root mean square speed of nitrogen at room temperature is about five hundred metres per second. Collisions with the walls transfer momentum, and averaging that transfer over the Maxwell distribution recovers the pressure of the ideal gas law. Between collisions a molecule travels a mean free path that grows as the density falls, which sets the scale for viscosity, diffusion and thermal conduction in dilute gases. Effusion through a small hole, studied by Graham, selects faster molecules and was used to separate isotopes. All of these results follow from treating the molecules as independent classical particles with random velocities, the same assumptions that define the ideal gas.

gas.label: gas/1.1
gas.text:
Pressure is the momentum delivered per unit time and per unit area by molecules striking the walls of the container. Each impact reverses the normal component of a molecular velocity, and the rate of impacts grows with density and speed, so pressure grows with both.

[formula]

A mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of a mercury column, about seven hundred sixty millimetres at sea level. The SI unit of pressure is the pascal, one newton per square metre, and one standard atmosphere is about one hundred kilopascals.

entropy.label: entropy/2
entropy.text:
Entropy is a state function that counts, on a logarithmic scale, the microscopic arrangements of a system.

The second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. For a reversible exchange of heat dQ at temperature T the entropy changes by dQ over T, while for an irreversible process the Clausius inequality gives a strictly larger entropy change than the heat exchanged divided by the temperature. Mixing two different gases, letting a gas expand freely into a vacuum, and conducting heat across a finite temperature difference are all irreversible and raise the total entropy. Because entropy is a state function, the change between two equilibrium states can be computed along any convenient reversible path, even when the actual process was irreversible. Equilibrium of an isolated system is reached when the entropy is as large as the constraints allow, and this maximum principle is the starting point for the stability conditions on heat capacities and compressibilities. In statistical mechanics the same quantity reappears as the logarithm of the number of accessible microstates, which connects the thermodynamic arrow of time to probability.

entropy.label: entropy/2.1-d0
entropy.text: Boltzmann's formula S = k log W relates the entropy to the number W of microstates compatible with the macroscopic state. It is engraved on his tombstone in Vienna and is the bridge between counting configurations and measuring heat.

entropy.label: entropy/2.1-x
entropy.text: Gibbs generalized the counting to systems whose microstates have unequal probabilities: the entropy is minus k times the sum over states of p log p. For equal probabilities this reduces to Boltzmann's formula, and for a system in contact with a heat bath it yields the canonical entropy. Shannon later found the same expression as the measure of missing information in a message, so the information entropy of a source and the thermodynamic entropy of a gas share one mathematical form. The Gibbs expression is maximized, subject to fixed average energy, by the Boltzmann distribution, which is one way to derive the canonical ensemble without appealing to a heat bath. Maximum entropy inference uses the same idea for incomplete data in many other fields, such as image reconstruction and ecology, where only a few averages are known and every other assumption should be avoided.

entropy.label: entropy/2.2-list
entropy.text:
Entropy approaches a constant value as the temperature approaches absolute zero.

Heat capacities and thermal expansion coefficients vanish at absolute zero.

Absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of cooling steps.

entropy.label: entropy/v2/3-a1
entropy.text: Heat engines and refrigerators are governed by an entropy balance. An engine takes heat from a hot reservoir, rejects part of it to a cold reservoir and converts the difference into work; because the entropy taken from the hot side cannot exceed the entropy given to the cold side, the efficiency is at most one minus the ratio of the cold to the hot temperature, the Carnot efficiency. A heat pump runs the cycle backwards and needs work to move heat from cold to hot. Real machines fall short of the Carnot limit because friction and finite temperature differences generate entropy.

entropy.label: entropy/3-a2
entropy.text: In chemistry the direction of a reaction at constant temperature and pressure is decided by the Gibbs free energy, G = H - TS. A reaction proceeds spontaneously when it lowers G, so a reaction that absorbs heat can still run if it increases the entropy enough, as when ice melts above zero degrees Celsius or salt dissolves in water and cools the solution. Entropy therefore decides chemical equilibrium as much as energy does.
